As cars become increasingly software-defined, owning a vehicle no longer necessarily means having full access to the technology that makes it function. Proprietary diagnostic protocols, software restrictions and increasingly complex electronics have made it harder for everyday drivers to understand, customise and repair their vehicles independently.

Lithuanian automotive technology company OBDeleven is building a business around changing that. Founded in 2014 and headquartered in Kaunas, its technology combines a compact Bluetooth-enabled device that plugs into a vehicle's OBD-II port with a smartphone app, enabling drivers to identify faults, monitor vehicle health, access real-time performance data and customise vehicle features without specialist equipment.

Originally established as Voltas IT, the bootstrapped company has expanded beyond automotive enthusiasts to target everyday drivers, positioning itself as a comprehensive digital car ownership platform. OBDeleven has connected more than 6 million vehicles across over 60 countries. In 2025, the company generated €19.2 million in revenue, representing 25 per cent year-on-year growth, and recorded a net profit of €3.17 million. It has established partnerships with major automotive manufacturers, including Volkswagen Group, BMW Group, Toyota Group, Ford US and Mercedes-Benz.

I spoke to Juozapas “Joe” Preikša, CMO of OBDeleven, during a trip to Vilnius earlier this year to learn more.

How increasingly complex vehicles challenge the right to repair

Over the years, I've written about how the car-hacking community helps drive the right-to-repair movement, raising a key question: what happens when you own a car but not the software that makes it function?

Many car owners have fond memories of buying an older car in early adulthood and spending hours happily tinkering under the bonnet, exploring and learning by taking things apart and putting them back together. Today, you're increasingly likely to use code rather than a spanner. As vehicles become more software-defined, mechanical tinkering has given way to navigating electronic control units, diagnostic codes and software configurations. Much of this functionality has historically required expensive, manufacturer-specific diagnostic equipment or specialist technical knowledge.

However, a love of cars has resulted in an underground movement of sorts in garages, car parks and maker spaces, where car hackers seek to understand what their vehicles can do and what they could do through modifications to their hardware or software. Examples include OpenGarages, a network of automotive enthusiasts, hobbyists and security researchers, and the Car Hacking Village, which brings together automotive cybersecurity enthusiasts at industry events like CES and Defcon.

Preikša points to the growing complexity of modern vehicles as another barrier to independent repairs.

“Nowadays, you open up the bonnet and see a big piece of plastic. You have thousands of sensors, and you have no idea where any of them are. If you want to change some of them, it's an engine-out job.”

Identifying a faulty sensor increasingly requires diagnostic tools rather than physical inspection. However, accessing this information requires knowledge of the specific electronic addresses associated with individual sensors — information that is typically proprietary to the vehicle manufacturer. While reverse engineering is possible, Preikša explains that mapping the thousands of sensors within a modern vehicle is a complex and time-consuming process.

Even when a fault has been identified, manufacturers can impose additional restrictions on what users can do.

“Then, when you try to do something about it, they say, ‘Hold on, you will need to get an authentication code.’”

OBDeleven represents the commercial evolution of some of these grassroots efforts, making vehicle diagnostics, coding and customisation accessible to everyday motorists through their smartphones. However, it does so by cooperating with automotive manufacturers rather than positioning itself as a way to circumvent them.

Why making vehicle diagnostics accessible is no easy task

Despite the existence of a standardised vehicle diagnostics protocol, OBD-II, automotive manufacturers continue to rely heavily on proprietary systems. This creates significant barriers for independent diagnostic providers seeking to offer comprehensive functionality across multiple vehicle brands.

“Every single automotive manufacturer changes the protocols. They're proprietary, and there's always the big question of how much they will open up,” explained Preikša.

While OBD-II standardises aspects of the physical diagnostic connection and how diagnostic devices communicate with vehicles, manufacturers typically limit standardised access to emissions-related information, such as oxygen sensor faults and engine misfires.

“Manufacturers, I don't know why, do the bare minimum on that protocol.”

Preikša contends that manufacturers could make a much broader range of vehicle systems accessible through a common protocol, including airbags and other electronic components, reducing the need for brand-specific diagnostic solutions.

“Essentially, all of the brands could put everything under one open protocol, and it would work 90 per cent of the time.

Then you would have to add that 10 per cent of proprietary stuff. They're doing the opposite.”

The economics of keeping drivers dependent on dealerships

While OBDeleven offers a range of vehicle customisation and monitoring capabilities, diagnostics remains its most popular application.

“Diagnostics is our bread and butter. Our price point, our size and our capabilities allow an everyday driver to understand what a warning light is about.”

Despite the increasing sophistication of in-car displays, manufacturers often provide little information about the underlying cause of a fault, instead directing drivers to authorised repair centres.

Preikša explained:

“It's easier to say, ‘Go visit the workshop right now,’ and give you five options for BMW workshops around you. It keeps them in business.”

He points to discussions at a recent automotive industry conference in the UK, where he heard that dealerships typically make just £300 to £500 from the sale of a vehicle, even for relatively expensive models. With such narrow margins, financing, maintenance and servicing become increasingly important sources of revenue.

“That's why they try to include financing and push service subscriptions. You see how they're trying to pull the driver back to the official dealer to maintain the car there, so the dealer network has its revenue.”

For independent diagnostic providers like OBDeleven, this creates a commercial opportunity: giving drivers greater visibility into their vehicle's health and enabling them to make more informed decisions about where and when to seek repairs.

Bootstrapping a Lithuanian automotive scaleup

OBDeleven's growth is particularly noteworthy given that the company has been entirely bootstrapped. Founded by two brothers and a cousin, its origins lie in Lithuania's automotive repair industry. The brothers were highly skilled automotive electronics mechanics working at a Volkswagen workshop before leaving to establish their own business, specialising in coding, reverse engineering and complex electrical engineering. The inspiration for OBDeleven came from observing how cumbersome conventional vehicle diagnostic equipment was.

“Every single day, somebody would come to their shop and bring this huge laptop with a dongle to the car,” recalled Preikša.

“One of the guys said, ‘I already have the phone. You could work on the phone. It doesn't need that much processing power.’”

The founders bought a Chinese dongle and reverse-engineered some of its functionality, pooling their personal savings of approximately €10,000 to purchase an initial batch of devices. Demand quickly validated their approach.

“It was around €50,000 in revenue the first year, then €150,000, then €300,000, then €800,000, then a million. That's how it grew ever since, with a 25 to 30 per cent revenue growth rate.”

Today, the US is OBDeleven's biggest market, followed by the UK, Germany and the Netherlands.

From portable diagnostics to unlocking hidden vehicle features

OBDeleven initially gained traction among automotive enthusiasts by making vehicle diagnostics more accessible and portable. Replacing the laptop with a smartphone meant drivers could run diagnostics independently, wherever they were.

“With the mobility of the device, you could just keep it in your glovebox and do your diagnostics at home,” recalled Preikša.

However, the ability to customise vehicles and unlock hidden features proved equally important in attracting early adopters. OBDeleven initially focused on Volkswagen Group, which had begun integrating powerful electronic control units (ECUs) across its vehicle range. Different models often shared the same hardware, but software configurations determined which features drivers could access.

“You could have the same ECU in a Polo, a Golf, a Passat and a Phaeton. For some features, it was agnostic. You could actually activate features that were meant for a Passat or a Phaeton in the cheapest model. This got the attention, and this is how enthusiasts started using OBDeleven.”

Interestingly, OBDeleven originally marketed its device on eBay by advertising individual features that users could unlock. Preikša recalled:

“We had thousands of listings for individual features. It was just trying to get that feature into somebody's head because no one else had done that before.

Afterwards, we started to get traction in the Volkswagen Group community.”

To make vehicle customisation accessible to users without specialist coding knowledge, OBDeleven introduced One-Click Apps, automating the process of modifying vehicle software configurations.

“These are essentially applications where you just click, and the configuration in the settings changes in the background and activates something that's not normally on the car.”

OBDeleven offers more than 10,000 One-Click Apps, ranging from modifying exterior lighting, dashboard displays and multimedia startup animations to unlocking hidden manufacturer features and performing maintenance functions such as service resets. Available for selected Volkswagen Group, BMW, Toyota, Ford and Mercedes-Benz vehicles, the apps can be accessed using in-app credits or through OBDeleven's Ultimate subscription.

OBDeleven helped broaden its appeal beyond experienced automotive enthusiasts to drivers looking to personalise their vehicles. One of Preikša's favourite examples is changing regional lighting configurations.

“In modern cars, you have these beautiful taillight signatures, but during the daytime, they're off. I like to activate those. It's not meant for the Lithuanian market; it's meant for the Scandinavian markets, but we can activate it here. This is one of the more popular features you can enable for your car.

That's essentially what we do a lot of the time — change the regional configuration.”

Building relationships with automotive manufacturers

I was curious about how OBDeleven approached relationships with automotive manufacturers, particularly when it came to accessing proprietary data. According to Preikša, the company took an unconventional approach: it went directly to the manufacturers and offered to pay for access to their technical documentation.

“We were the first to approach Volkswagen and say, ‘Could you really give us the documentation? We'd like to pay you money.’ “They were like, ‘What?’”
